newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives slam Labour spending plans.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives slam Labour spending plans.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, trailing badly in opinion polls ahead of national elections, on Wednesday reached for a trusted vote-winning formula by accusing their Labour opponents of extravagant spending plans.
The party published a 100-page document which it claimed showed the Labour Party had already promised to increase government spending by 30 billion pounds ($50 billion) a year.
Labour, which under economics spokesman Gordon Brown has rigorously avoided specific spending pledges swiftly dismissed the claims as lies.
"What we see here is the same old Tory lie machine coming up with half-baked things that have no foundation whatsoever," finance spokesman Alistair Darling said.

But senior treasury minister William Waldegrave told a news conference that a future Labour government would have to raise the standard rate of income tax by nine pence in the pound to 33 pence, and raise higher tax rates to 70 pence in the pound.
The extra taxes would cost the average British family some 1,200 pounds ($2,017) over the next five years, he added.
"For all the rhetoric, New Labour remains the party of tax and spend," Waldegrave said.

The narrow Conservative victory at the last general election in 1992 came after an onslaught by the party on Labour's spending plans which it then claimed would cost taxpayers 37 billion pounds a year.

But the ruling party is in a much deeper electoral hole now than it was then, with opinion polls showing it some 20 points adrift of Labour and an election due by May 22. To compile the Conservative document, said Waldegrave, ministers and their political aides supplied civil servants with pledges made by Labour leaders, and, in many cases, their assumptions on what precisely they meant.
For instance, Labour is committed to introducing a minimum wage, but has avoided saying at what level it will be set.
After ministers suggested the level would be half average male earnings, the civil servants calculated the cost to the public sector pay bill at 3.7 billion pounds a year.
But Waldegrave insisted the estimates the party produced were modest. "The figures are, if anything, an underestimate of the true cost of Labour's promises," he said.

Prime Minister John Major said in an interview with the Press Association news agency: "We've only put in what is a copper-bottomed, clear-cut quote and promise, and we've added up what those amount to, and they do amount to an astonishing sum."
Labour, however, protested at the Conservative claims that the spending pledges had been costed by civil servants.
Darling said the party had contacted Sir Robin Butler, head of the civil service, who had "made it clear that this is not the case".

"It is...shocking that the Tory Party in this case should claim that civil servants had been involved as they described in order to give the exercise spurious authority," Darling said. ($1=.5950 Sterling)
